result.summary: The dead seer Amphiaraus arrives in the underworld, where Dis rages and orders Tisiphone to make a new horror. The Argives mourn him and appoint Thiodamas as their augur, while Thebes feasts. In the next day's battle Tydeus rampages, is mortally wounded by Melanippus, and gnaws his killer's head, so that Minerva flees in disgust.

scenes.title: Amphiaraus before the lord of Erebus
scenes.summary: The living prophet falls into the underworld and terrifies the shades. Dis rages and calls on Tisiphone to send a horror, but he spares Amphiaraus after the seer pleads.
scenes.stakes: Amphiaraus risks the wrath of the lord of the dead, who resents the intrusion.

scenes.title: The Argive camp mourns the seer
scenes.summary: The chariot is gone, Palaemon reports the chasm, and the troops flee. In camp the Argives lament Amphiaraus until sleep comes.
scenes.stakes: The Argives lose their prophet and their courage and the gods' favour.

scenes.title: Thebes feasts
scenes.summary: The Thebans celebrate and tell old tales of their city. Oedipus joins the banquet, secretly delighted at the prospect of more war between his sons.

scenes.title: Thiodamas named augur
scenes.summary: Adrastus watches in dismay and calls a council at dawn. Thiodamas is chosen as augur and prays to Earth and the lost Amphiaraus.
scenes.stakes: The Argives need a prophet; Thiodamas fears being unequal to the office.

scenes.title: The battle joined
scenes.summary: Thebes pours out of its seven gates and the armies clash. Tydeus and Haemon fight, Pallas and Hercules make peace, and Tydeus kills Atys.
scenes.stakes: Warriors on both sides face death in the open field.

scenes.title: Ismene and the dying Atys
scenes.summary: Antigone and Ismene talk in the palace, and Ismene tells of a dream. Atys is carried in dying and sees Ismene before the end.

scenes.title: Death of Tydeus
scenes.summary: Tydeus drives the Thebans back and hunts Eteocles. Melanippus wounds him, and Tydeus gnaws his killer's head, so Pallas flees.
scenes.stakes: Tydeus is dying and loses Pallas' promised immortality.

notable_quotes.reason: Dramatic opening: the living prophet bursts into the underworld with his armour.
Chilling comment on Tydeus' cannibal act before Tisiphone's demand.

analysis.text: Divine wrath and fury drive the war onward; even the underworld is provoked to produce new horrors.
The poem draws on Roman epic conventions: underworld scenes and battle catalogues echoing Virgil.

language_notes.text: Yew-branch purification and marking the door-post are rites of admitting the newly dead; Amphiaraus has not undergone them, so he is irregular among the shades.
Parcae: the Roman name for the Fates, who spin and cut the thread of each life.
The 'pale furrower' is Charon, ferryman of the Styx; the river is 'not his own' because Amphiaraus arrived by a chasm, not his ferry.
The 'third hazard' is the lot-drawing among the brothers, in which Dis received the underworld while Jove got heaven.
The 'Arcadian' is Mercury, who travels between worlds; the sons of Tyndareus, Castor and Pollux, share their time between the living and the dead.
Pirithous, Theseus and Alcides (Hercules) were living intruders into the underworld; Hercules carried off Cerberus.
The Odrysian plaint is Orpheus' song, a Thracian lament, which moved the Furies to tears when he sought Eurydice.
Dis abducted Proserpine from Sicily; Jove decreed she spend only half the year with him, at her mother Ceres' urging.
Piling Pelion on Ossa refers to the Giants' attempt to storm heaven.
Dictean judge: Minos, of Crete (Dicte is a Cretan mountain), a judge of the dead.
The Dorian land means Argos and the Peloponnese, the Argives' homeland; Palaemon fears it too may have vanished.
Oeclides is Amphiaraus, son of Oecles, the seer swallowed by the earth.
Tyrians here means Thebans, since Theban founder Cadmus came from Tyre. Vesper is the evening star.
The Castalian spring, grotto and tripod are Apollo's oracle at Delphi, whose god Amphiaraus served.
The Parcae are the Roman Fates, who spin and determine human destiny.
The lord of Avernus is Pluto, king of the underworld; Avernus is an entrance to it.
Tenedos, Chryse, Delos, Branchus' shrine, Clarus, Dindymus and the Lycian god name Apollo's oracular sites, which the soldiers say will fall silent.
Tiphys was helmsman of the Argo; the Minyae were its crew. His sudden death left the ship without a guide.
Sidonian: Theban, from Sidon, because Cadmus, Thebes' founder, came from Phoenicia. Idaean drums are those of Mount Ida's Cybele-worship.
Recalls Thebes' founding myths: Jove as a bull carrying off Europa, Cadmus following a heifer and sowing dragon's teeth, and Amphion's lyre raising the walls.
Oedipus lives in blind seclusion after discovering his incest and blinding himself; the 'blood' recalls that act.
Dis is the god of the underworld; Oedipus has long cursed him and the Furies.
Phineus was a blind king tormented by the Harpies, who snatched his food; the Argonauts drove them off.
Ships carried a tutelary god's image, named for the vessel; the god keeps watch with the helmsman.
Phoebus' fiery sister is the Moon (Diana), retreating as the Sun's horses rise from Ocean at dawn.
Amphiaraus, the Argive seer, was swallowed by the earth alive; Thiodamas is his fellow augur and successor.
Cirrha is near Delphi, home of Phoebus' oracle; Amphiaraus' chasm is likened to an oracular cleft.
Tisiphone is one of the Furies. Cithaeron and the towers (Thebes' walls, raised by Amphion's lyre) were used to far gentler music.
The list names Thebes' seven gates and their commanders; each gate faced one Argive champion. Ogygian is a poetic adjective for Thebes, from the old king Ogyges.
'Lord of the tripods' is Amphiaraus, the augur swallowed by the earth; tripods were seats of Apollo's prophecy. Thiodamas is his successor.
The Parrhasian cluster is the Great Bear or Wain; Parrhasia in Arcadia is linked to Callisto, who became the Bear. The missing star stands for Amphiaraus.
The Fates spin, measure and cut life's threads; here the Furies seize the threads, so deaths come before their time.
'Their groans reek' means the warriors' breath, mingled in the close fighting, steams in the air.
'Winged with a double death' probably describes arrows killing twice, perhaps poisoned or barbed; the original note flags a difficulty.
Twin brothers on opposite sides kill each other's twins, unrecognised under helmets; 'Cadmus' blood' means Thebans, descendants of the city's founder.
Pallas (Athena) supports Haemon, while Hercules (the Tirynthian, from Tiryns) supports Tydeus, though Haemon was Hercules' ward by upbringing (see 134).
The Helicaons were born to a priestess against Venus' will, implying broken vows; their mother now prays at altars unaware they are dead.
Hypanis and Polites were consecrated: one kept his beard for Phoebus (Apollo), the other his hair for Iacchus (Bacchus). Youths offered grown hair to gods.
Inachian means Argive, from Inachus, the river-god and legendary first king of Argos; Ismenian and Cadmean mean Theban.
Tirynthian is Hercules, who was reared at Tiryns; he calls Pallas 'sister' as a fellow child of Jove.
Hercules' labours, in which Pallas helped him, and his descent to Tartarus; Hyllus was his son, Amphitryon his mortal stepfather. Hercules disowns Tydeus' foes, Thebes.
Acheloian refers to Tydeus, from Aetolia, where the river Achelous flows.
Tritonia is a title of Pallas (Minerva), linked to Lake Triton or the river Triton.
Oenides, 'son of Oeneus,' is Tydeus; horn-footed means hooved.
Ismene, daughter of Oedipus, is here called offspring of Agenor, an ancestor of the Theban line; her kin's 'evil deeds' refer to Thebes' cursed house.
The syntax slips: 'nor to crouch' continues the idea 'he is mad to drench himself... and to crouch only on a chief bull's neck.'
Pandion's birds are Procne and Philomela, his daughters, turned into swallow and nightingale after the Tereus story; their wordless cries are the 'old story of their woe'.
Her dream-vision is confused: fire falls between the pair and Atys's mother pursues her, demanding him back, foretelling his death.
'Dorian host' means the Argive (Greek) army besieging Thebes; the poet uses 'Dorian' loosely for the invaders.
'Outside the shield' means he is carried lying on his shield, the usual way of bearing a fallen warrior; his neck hangs over its edge.
'Son-in-law' is used because Atys was betrothed to Ismene, Jocasta's daughter.
Oenides means 'son of Oeneus', a patronymic for Tydeus. Aonian means Theban, from Aonia, a region of Boeotia.
Tydeus recalls his earlier embassy to Thebes, when he killed fifty ambushers and was spared to return to Mycenae (Inachian means Argive).
Eteocles is saved for the fratricidal duel with his brother Polynices, which fate has already set.
Pallas and Tritonia are names for Minerva's Greek counterpart Athena; her 'mighty sire' is Jove.
The Tirynthian is Hercules, who carried the Erymanthian boar alive to Eurystheus at Mycenae or Argos.
Tydeus's cannibal act horrifies Pallas, who had meant to make him immortal; she needs ritual purification at Athens, where the Ilissus (Elisos) flows.

context_notes.text: Amphiaraus, an Argive seer, was swallowed alive with his chariot by an earth chasm during the battle at Thebes.
The lord of Erebus is Dis, the king of the underworld, brother of Jove.
Tisiphone is one of the Furies, here summoned to inspire the brothers Eteocles and Polynices to fratricide.
His wife Eriphyle took a golden necklace as a bribe to make him join the doomed war against Thebes.
Amphiaraus, an Argive seer, was swallowed by the earth while fighting at Thebes, which is why his chariot is sought in vain.
Adrastus is king of Argos and leader of the expedition against Thebes.
Mopsus is a seer and Actor a warrior in the Argive army.
Tiresias was Thebes' famous blind prophet, whom the Thebans praise against the Argive augur Amphiaraus.
Adrastus is king of Argos and leader of the Greek host against Thebes; he is old and burdened.
Earth is invoked because she swallowed Amphiaraus; Prometheus' men and Pyrrha's stones refer to myths of humanity's creation and renewal after the flood.
Burying black sheep alive is a rite for the dead, here honoring Amphiaraus as if he were a chthonic power.
Bellona is the Roman goddess of war, here assaulting the gates as the armies emerge.
The War-god is Mars; his spear is still 'dry' because no blood has yet been shed.
Menalcas is a Spartan; Taygetus is the mountain range beside Sparta, and Spartans prized dying with wounds in front.
Pisa (Olympia) is sacred to Jupiter and Cirrha to Apollo's Delphi, so the fallen men are worshippers of rival gods.
Hercules, born in Thebes, supports Haemon and the Thebans, while Pallas favours Tydeus; the gods' rival loyalties set up the confrontation.
Snakes fringe Pallas' aegis, which bristles when she is angry.
Uranie is the Muse of astronomy; Corymbus came from Helicon, mountain of the Muses.
Menoeceus is a Theban noble who in this poem will later sacrifice himself for the city.
Antigone and Ismene are daughters of Oedipus and Jocasta, sisters of the warring brothers Eteocles and Polynices.
The exile is Polynices, who leads the Argive attack on Thebes; Eteocles holds the throne.
Closing the eyes of the dead was a customary duty of close kin.
Enyo is a Greek war goddess, here a fury-like figure who rekindles the battle.
Melanippus is a Theban warrior whose spear gives Tydeus his fatal wound.
Tisiphone is one of the Furies, here driving Tydeus to his savage act.

literary_notes.text: Meres and lakes 'resound with groaning' and Charon cries out, making the landscape itself react in alarm.
Dis is shown as pitiless, wrathful even at his own subjects, which sets up his violent outburst.
Dis's string of questions displays his paranoid, wounded pride and his rivalry with Jove.
Dis's shaking of the realm is compared to Jupiter's nod moving heaven, equating the two brothers' power.
Fading armour, dim fillet and dying olive show the seer's dignity lingering as he becomes a shade.
The lion that spares a fallen foe illustrates Dis's reluctant mercy, angry yet satisfied by submission.
Palaemon's panic makes even the solid field seem to flee, conveying how the earth's collapse has shaken all certainty.
Rumour is pictured as a bold agent who actively spreads new terrors.
The horses seem to know the horror and refuse commands, as if sharing the men's dread.
The string of neglected routines, listed without conjunctions, shows the soldiers' numb despair.
The lament's questions reproach Apollo and turn grief into accusation against the gods.
The army without Amphiaraus is compared to the Argo bereft of Tiphys, showing the loss of its guide.
The Thebans misread Oedipus' cheer, while the reader knows he rejoices in the coming strife between his sons.
Oedipus' unexplained joy is compared to Phineus' wary relief after his torment ended.
Theban noise and torches set against Adrastus' anxious wakefulness sharpens the camp's gloom.
Adrastus is the lone watchful helmsman while others sleep trustingly.
Thiodamas' awed reluctance is likened to a young Persian prince inheriting a throne he fears to fill.
Thiodamas addresses Earth directly and reproaches her, making her a listening, answerable goddess.
Earth is asked to hold back and not hasten the Fates, treating her as a being who can be persuaded.
The Nile's seven mouths in flood mirror the seven gates disgorging armies; the sea creatures' fear echoes the Argives' dread.
Death is given jaws, a bloody nail and a choosy appetite, making the slaughter feel deliberate and predatory.
The gleaming order of the lines is tinged with foreboding: the beauty described is about to be destroyed by blood.
The battle's shifting advance and retreat are likened to Auster and Aquilo, opposing winds, fighting in the sky until one wins.
The severed arm still gripping its sword, and a man striking it, grotesquely exaggerates the frenzy of the battle.
Tydeus is compared to a tigress eager for blood, stressing his bestial ferocity.
Haemon's lost nerve is compared to a boar grazed by a javelin, which has learned to fear the spear and loses its fury.
The fall of horse and rider is likened to an elm dragging down its vine, giving pathos to the rider's death.
The poet-warrior sought battle for song material and becomes the subject of song himself, while the Muses mourn silently.
'Trusting alas!' signals that Atys' golden finery and confidence will lead to his doom.
Atys is compared to a young lion with an unripe mane, attacking weak prey before he meets a real adversary.
Tydeus' terrible laugh and careless, almost contemptuous throw show his savage confidence, and the fatal result shows his strength.
Tydeus is likened to a lion ignoring small prey and seeking a chieftain bull, showing his appetite for great victims.
The sisters' sorrowful, half-spoken talk is compared to the swallows' mournful twittering, which sounds like speech but is only lament.
The dream's fire and the mother demanding Atys back anticipate his death in the next lines.
Atys's repeated struggle to lift his eyes to Ismene, ignoring the light of life, makes his death moving.
Tydeus swooping on Eteocles is compared to Jove's eagle attacking a swan, stressing speed and predatory menace.
The wolf ignoring the shepherds and pursuing only his chosen prey mirrors Tydeus single-mindedly hunting Eteocles.
The Mars figure on the helmet falls, a bad omen: the war god's own emblem abandons the warrior.
The parenthetical 'what fiery zeal!' shows the narrator's admiration for Tydeus's refusal to die.
The Gorgon-head's serpents rear up as if alive, shading the goddess's face and showing her horror.
